9.0.s.en: (1) The healing of the man born blind

9.0.0.en: "Blind from his birth": that is, he had no eyes at all. This makes the coming miracle fall not under the miracles of healing but under the miracles of creation. As for the question that the disciples asked the Lord Christ, inquiring about the cause of this man's blindness, it expresses the belief of the Jews, and their faith in what came in the Law, that God visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, or that illness is a direct result of sin. But God also permits trials and illnesses for His righteous children and saints, to show virtues such as thanksgiving and endurance, and He permits other illnesses for sinners for the purpose of their repentance and return.

9.1.0.en: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents": this answer from the Lord Christ to His disciples was to turn them away from searching for causes, and to prepare them to receive the coming work of God. For the blind man here represents a field for the manifestation, not only of a specific work that God the Word performs, but it reveals to us the attributes and the dispensation of the Son toward all His creation; for we find the attribute of tenderness and fatherly love in God who visits His weak creation, for it is Christ who went to the blind man, the Samaritan woman and the paralytic, and they did not come to Him. Likewise the attribute of creation, which is a work in which Christ declares His divinity and His own power to create an eye out of nothing, with all it includes of tissues and nerves and the power of sight. And finally, the Son also declares the relationship between Himself and the Father in will and work in (v. 4). And the last of the purposes of this miracle is the faith in Christ of everyone who saw it, in view of its difficulty.

9.1.1.en: "While it is day": a reference to His bodily life on earth, and the night is the end of life and death. And this message is directed to all of us, beloved, for Christ is speaking about all of us, because the day is my life and your life. And we are called to use this day, before our life passes, in doing good. It is a great opportunity for us to do in it the works of God, because death comes, and then there is no benefit in us after the opportunity is lost, indeed regret for wasting our life on other things, such as pleasures or preoccupation with the affairs of the world, will profit nothing. So let us make use of this precious opportunity in positive work, and goodness, and the service of the Lord. "I am the light of the world": that is, Christ is the only source of illumination for everyone who lives in the blindness and darkness of sin, and there is no light or savior other than Him. And there has already been discussion in (ch. 8) of Christ as the light of the world. As for enjoying this light, its only entrance is the life of repentance, and fellowship with Christ in His Church.

9.2.0.en: It is wonderful that the Lord should use clay, which damages the eye, in healing and creating the eye.

9.2.1.en: And St. John Chrysostom says that Christ shows that His power in healing diseases exceeds the powers of nature, and proves that He is not bound to one means in performing His miracles, for sometimes He heals by the word, at other times by touch, and at others by spitting on the dust, and so on...

9.2.2.en: "Go, wash": that is, the healing begins with washing, and washing is the act of repentance. And in our faith, Baptism is a washing from sin, "that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" (Eph 5:26). Therefore Baptism was the door of Christianity, because it is the entrance of salvation...

9.2.3.en: Likewise, dealing with the Holy Bible and the word of God is a second source of spiritual washing and purification of the soul.

9.2.4.en: And the third source is repentance and the sacrament of confession. For repentance and confession are a daily Baptism, in which a person is washed from his sins, and by them receives the gift of healing and the salvation of the soul. As for the word "Go," and the words "went his way and washed," they are a clear reference to the human role; for he was blind. And it would have been easier for Christ to heal him without burdening him with the toil of the way to the pool, while he still could not see, and the return from it seeing. But Christ wants to declare that, although the gifts of healing (Baptism) and salvation are free, there is a role and a responsibility on man in going and returning. And this is what we call "spiritual striving in the life with God." And the blessings of obedience, faith, the washing of Baptism, and man's striving were crowned with sight and enlightenment.

9.2.5.en: And this is also available to each one of us, if he accepts and does as this man did, and obeys Christ, and holds fast to the means of grace in His Church.

9.3.0.en: The crowd took the man born blind to the Pharisees, who in the eyes of the Jews were the most learned of people and the teachers of the Law, seeking an explanation for this unique wonder. And St. John mentioned that the miracle took place on a Sabbath, in preparation for what the Pharisees would say in (v. 16) on the one hand, and to confirm Christ's teaching that the Sabbath does not nullify the work of mercy on the other; which Christ had done and taught in all the previous healing miracles.

9.3.1.en: "Then again the Pharisees also asked him": it means that the Pharisees had heard the story from the crowd. But, for further investigation and clarification, they asked the man concerned himself, and their motive was jealousy and hatred toward the Lord Christ, and an attempt to find a charge against Him, and not to believe the fact and acknowledge it.

9.3.2.en: And often, beloved, our prejudgments about people lead us to deviate from the truth, despite its clarity, because of the feelings with which our souls are filled toward them that do not please God.

9.4.0.en: The Pharisees were divided in their opinion, for the majority, who wanted to condemn Christ, closed their eyes to the miracle and its power, and saw nothing but that Christ was a breaker of the commandment to keep the Sabbath. But a few of them could do nothing but declare their rejection of the first opinion; is it reasonable that a sinful man should do what no one can do but God?

9.4.1.en: And therefore the division occurred, and the council of the Pharisees did not come out with one opinion.

9.5.0.en: And with this division, they put a question to the blind man himself about his personal opinion of what had happened, hoping they might find in his words a pretext by which to accuse Christ of sorcery, or something that would cast doubt on the occurrence of a miracle.

9.5.1.en: But the answer of the blind man, who acknowledged the favor of the One who had brought light into his life, came as a disappointment to all their hopes, for he declared his faith that He is a prophet, showing thereby courage and love of the truth, for he bears witness to Christ before a council that he knows is mostly against Christ.

9.6.0.en: Since the blind man's testimony was not to the Pharisees' liking, they summoned his parents, as a last hope of denying this miracle, and they put their question in a disapproving form, so that they would reject their son's statement. But his parents' answer was brief and decisive, for they acknowledged that the man was their son, and that he was born blind.

9.7.0.en: But at the same time, they declared that they did not know the events of the miracle, and this for two reasons; the first: that they had not actually seen it. The second, which is the more fitting, is what St. John mentions, that they feared that the Jews would put them out of the synagogue, which would result in their being deprived of religious rights and the practice of worship. And the punishment of expulsion from the synagogue was, in many cases, a prelude to another punishment, which was death. Therefore, they sent him back to the Pharisees to complete his questioning, as a man responsible for his own answer.

9.7.1.en: "He is of age": it means that he had passed thirty years of his life.

9.8.s.en: (4) The man born blind bears witness to Christ

9.8.0.en: "Give God the praise": it was a legal and religious procedure, like a kind of adjuration, obliging the one addressed to tell the truth. And it is a fearful expression in the soul of every Jew, for it usually preceded the religious trials that ended in the Jew's being banned from the synagogue, or delivered to death... see the story of "Achan the son of Carmi" (Josh 7:19). However, this questioning was not impartial, and its purpose was not to listen to the story in order to arrive at the truth, but the prior and evident condemnation of Christ in their suggestive words to the man, when they said: "We know that this man is a sinner."

9.8.1.en: But the man's answer came frank and simple: I am not concerned with your judgment of this man, for you see Him as a sinner, but I live a reality that I cannot deny, which is that yesterday I was living in darkness, and today I am in the light.

9.8.3.en: How sweet are these resounding words, whose echo is heard in the suffering soul. For often God opens our eyes and minds and hearts to mistakes we were committing, and had become accustomed to, as the blind man is accustomed to darkness. But after the entry of the divine light, and the illumination of the soul by the love of Christ, a person cannot accept the darkness of sin again. And in proportion as a person grows in life with God, and discovers new dimensions in the divine love, he can only repeat: "I was blind, now I see."

9.9.0.en: Once more the Pharisees return to a new questioning, hoping they might find something with which to overturn his testimony. But the man was overcome with distress at the attempt to pressure him and have his testimony repeated again and again, and expressed this distress with a certain biting sarcasm, when he said to them: perhaps the purpose of your many questions is to believe in Him, and to become His disciples?! Their answer came as a mixture of sin and arrogance; the sin is that they reviled him, and the arrogance is their vain boasting that they were disciples of Moses, and their considering discipleship to Christ an insult, which they ascribed to the man born blind.

9.10.0.en: The man marveled, and in this marveling there is a new sarcasm, as though he were saying: how is it that you do not know, when you claim to be the people of knowledge, especially since the event and the miracle are beyond human ability, for God spoke to Moses (v. 29), but he did not perform such works, so is not this One better than Moses, the object of your boasting?!

9.10.1.en: And the man also presented a new defense against the council of the Pharisees, which is: does God answer sinners?! Or is the one who does these works, and whom God hears, a righteous and godly man, who does the will of God and fulfills it in his life. And the man presents a final proof with which he concludes his speech, which is that it has never been heard in the whole history of mankind, since creation, that eyes were created for a man born blind. Consequently, the One who performed this miracle is not merely a righteous man, but is from God; as though this testimony had been put in his mouth by the Holy Spirit.

9.11.0.en: As for bearing witness to the truth, its reward was reviling and being cast out from before the council of inquiry, without greater condemnation, lest the people who believed in the miracle should rise up.

9.11.1.en: And we learn from the man born blind that bearing witness to the truth sometimes carries a heavy price, and none is able for it except the man who believes in the power of God and the support of the Holy Spirit for him, like all the martyrs of the Church whom neither pain nor fear deterred from proclaiming the truth, even if they paid their lives as the price for it.

9.12.s.en: (5) The difference between physical blindness and spiritual blindness

9.12.0.en: From our understanding of these verses, we find that Christ, to Him be glory, is the One who sought the man, and "found him." And the man carried the spirit of the glad tidings on the one hand, and the pain of expulsion on the other. But his perception was not complete, for the utmost he reached as a man was that Christ is a prophet. Therefore the Lord had to seek him out, to complete the enlightenment of his heart, as He had enlightened his eyes.

9.12.1.en: And Christ here uses an expression like the one He used before, for just as He said: "I am the light of the world," "I am the bread of life," which are expressions characterized by the declaration of His divinity, He says here: "It is He," which is the same style by which God described Himself to Moses, when Moses asked Him His name, and God said to him: "I AM THAT I AM," that is, the One who is and who will be. And this declaration from Christ was linked to a direct question to the man: "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?" Therefore the man's answer came, after inquiry, and Christ's declaration of Himself: "Lord, I believe," and he expressed his faith in Christ by worshipping Him. And so his inner sight was opened, and he saw God with his heart after having seen Him with his eyes.

9.13.0.en: "For judgment I am come": it means that I came to reveal what is in the hearts of people, and which of them accepts God and is enlightened by the knowledge of Him, or rejects Him and remains in darkness. For the Pharisees were the people most knowledgeable of the Law, but they did not accept the God of redemption and of the promises of whom their Law spoke. So Christ, the true Light, came to uncover their spiritual blindness. But the simple, who had no knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, came by faith to enjoy a spiritual sight higher in rank than any fleshly sight or knowledge. And here we remember what came in (ch. 3:19): "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil."

9.14.0.en: The Pharisees understood the point of Christ's words and His hint, so they asked Him directly: "Are we blind also?" (the scholars of the Law, who examine it and teach it), in an attempt to catch Him in a word. But Christ's answer came stronger and harsher than the Pharisees had expected, which is: if you were blind through ignorance of the Law, and had no ability to distinguish the lawful from the forbidden, or to distinguish the one sent from God from one who is not, you would have an excuse, and sin would not be reckoned against you. But your claim of knowledge is what condemns you, for you have persisted in your obstinacy and have not believed, despite the prophecies fulfilled in me, and the works that none can do but the Creator God. Therefore the judgment for your rejection of me remains on you.

9.14.1.en: O my God... give me this luminous spiritual sight, for I do not want my mind or my knowledge or my self to be obstacles preventing me from recognizing Your traces and Your works and Your voice in my life... For I do not want to be a Pharisee who claims to see, but a blind man who wants to see, trusting in his God, the only light of the world.

9.14.2.en: The parable of the good shepherd; the Son's relationship with the Father; the accusation against Christ of blasphemy
